content:
# Judith Chapter 10 — Disagreement Log
**Date:** 2026-03-17

---

## Summary
**Total Disagreements: 27**
Chapter 10 presents Judith's transformation from mourning widow to armed beauty, her departure from Bethulia, and her reception by the Assyrian forces. Disagreements concentrate in three areas: (1) the adornment scene and its vocabulary of beauty and deception (vv. 2-4); (2) the dialogue with the patrol (vv. 12-16), where Judith performs her deception for the first time; and (3) the soldiers' reactions (vv. 18-19), which assess Judith as a representative of her entire people.

---

## Disagreements

**1. v. 1 — Narrative introduction**
- EMET: "And it-came-to-pass, when she-had-ceased crying-out..."
- LOGOS: "When Judith had finished crying out to the God of Israel and had completed all these words,"
- PNEUMA: "When the last word of her prayer had left her lips,"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — preserves the full referent ("the God of Israel") and the completeness formula; PNEUMA's phrase is evocative but interpretive

**2. v. 2 — "put-off / took-off" the sackcloth**
- EMET: "put-off from-herself the sackcloth and took-off the garments of her widowhood"
- LOGOS: "took off the sackcloth and removed her widow's clothing"
- PNEUMA: "stripped off the sackcloth and shed her widow's clothes"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — "took off / removed" is appropriate without being overly dramatic; PNEUMA's "stripped" / "shed" may over-vivify

**3. v. 3 — "washed her body with water"**
- EMET: "washed her body with water"
- LOGOS: "bathed her body with water"
- PNEUMA: "washed herself clean"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — "bathed" is more dignified and precise than PNEUMA's paraphrase

**4. v. 3 — "anointed herself with rich myrrh"**
- EMET: "anointed herself with rich myrrh"
- LOGOS: "anointed herself with rich myrrh"
- PNEUMA: "rubbed rich myrrh into her skin"
- SOPHIA ruling: EMET/LOGOS — "anointed" preserves the ceremonial register; PNEUMA's "rubbed... into her skin" is too physical

**5. v. 3 — "plaited / dressed her hair"**
- EMET: "plaited the hairs of her head"
- LOGOS: "dressed her hair"
- PNEUMA: "braided her hair"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — "dressed her hair" is broad enough to cover *eplexen tas trichas* (lit. "plaited/arranged the hairs"); "plaited" (EMET) is technically accurate but dated

**6. v. 3 — "garments of her gladness"**
- EMET: "garments of her-gladness"
- LOGOS: "festive garments"
- PNEUMA: "beautiful clothes"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — "festive garments" is more precise; EMET's "garments of gladness" is the literal *himation euphrosynēs* and could be noted in footnotes

**7. v. 4 — "for-the-purpose-of deceiving the eyes"**
- EMET: "for-the-purpose-of deceiving the eyes of all the men who would see her"
- LOGOS: "in order to beguile the eyes of whatever men might see her"
- PNEUMA: "to catch the eye of any man who saw her" (softens "deceive" to "catch the eye")
- SOPHIA ruling: "to deceive the eyes of whatever men might see her" — *pros apatēn opthalmōn* = for the deception of eyes; PNEUMA's softening loses the deliberate deception vocabulary

**8. v. 4 — "she made herself very beautiful" vs. "making herself as beautiful as possible"**
- EMET: "she made-herself very beautiful"
- LOGOS: "making herself as beautiful as possible"
- PNEUMA: "made herself as beautiful as she knew how"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — "as beautiful as possible" renders *ekallopisen heautēn sphodra* well

**9. v. 4 — PNEUMA addition: "She was arming herself. Her beauty was her weapon."**
- EMET: (not present)
- LOGOS: (not present)
- PNEUMA: "She was arming herself. Her beauty was her weapon. Every ornament was calculated to catch the eye of any man who saw her."
- SOPHIA ruling: Not adopted — "weapon" is interpretively true but not in the Greek text; SOPHIA notes this in the Council Notes

**10. v. 5 — "a cake of dried-figs" / "cakes of dried figs"**
- EMET: "a cake of dried-figs"
- LOGOS: "cakes of dried figs"
- PNEUMA: "dried fig cakes"
- SOPHIA ruling: "cakes of dried figs" (LOGOS) — the Greek *palathōn* can be plural or collective

**11. v. 5 — "wrapped all her utensils"**
- EMET: "wrapped all her utensils together"
- LOGOS: "wrapped all her provisions together"
- PNEUMA: (absorbed into "packed")
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — "provisions" is more accurate than "utensils" (*skeuē* = implements/provisions/gear); PNEUMA abbreviates too much

**12. v. 7 — "her face was changed and her clothing was changed"**
- EMET: "her face was-changed and her clothing was-changed"
- LOGOS: "her face transformed and her clothing changed"
- PNEUMA: "Her face was different. Her clothes were different."
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — "transformed" for *metabeblēmenos* (lit. changed/transformed) is well-chosen; PNEUMA's short sentences are punchy but lose the parallel Greek structure

**13. v. 7 — "amazed exceedingly" / "utterly astonished"**
- EMET: "they-were-amazed exceedingly at her beauty"
- LOGOS: "they were utterly astonished at her beauty"
- PNEUMA: "they stood there, overcome by her beauty"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — "utterly astonished" renders *exestēsan sphodra* well; PNEUMA's "overcome" implies physical incapacity

**14. v. 8 — "accomplish your plan" vs. "fulfill your purpose"**
- EMET: (not specified — "accomplish your plan")
- LOGOS: "fulfill your purpose"
- PNEUMA: "see your plan through"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — "fulfill your purpose" is the most liturgically appropriate

**15. v. 9 — "command to open" / "order them to open"**
- EMET: "Command [them] to open for me the gate"
- LOGOS: "Order them to open the city gate for me"
- PNEUMA: "Open the gate" (direct command)
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — Judith speaks to the elders, not to the guards; the indirect command structure must be preserved

**16. v. 10 — "watched her until she passed through the valley"**
- EMET: "watched her until she went-down the mountain, until she passed-through the valley, and they were no longer able to see her"
- LOGOS: "watched her until she had descended the mountain, crossed through the valley, and passed beyond their sight"
- PNEUMA: "watched them go, watched them descend the slope, cross the valley, and finally disappear from sight"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — two stages (mountain descent + valley crossing); PNEUMA's "slope" for "mountain" loses some scale

**17. v. 12 — "daughter of the Hebrews" / "Hebrew woman"**
- EMET: "I am a daughter of the Hebrews"
- LOGOS: "I am a Hebrew woman"
- PNEUMA: "I am a Hebrew woman"
- SOPHIA ruling: EMET — "daughter of the Hebrews" (*thugatēr Hebraiōn*) is the literal and theologically resonant form; it echoes OT usage

**18. v. 12 — "they are about to be given to you for plunder"**
- EMET: "they are-about to-be-given to you for-plunder"
- LOGOS: "they are about to be handed over to you as plunder"
- PNEUMA: "they are about to be handed over to you"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — "handed over as plunder" preserves *eis diarpagēn* = for plundering/as plunder; PNEUMA omits

**19. v. 13 — "to report true words" / "to deliver true intelligence"**
- EMET: "to report true words"
- LOGOS: "to deliver true intelligence"
- PNEUMA: "I have intelligence for him"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — "true intelligence" is appropriately ironic given her intended deception; EMET's "true words" is literal but less crisp

**20. v. 14 — "wonderfully beautiful" / "exceedingly beautiful" / "strikingly beautiful"**
- EMET: "wonderfully-beautiful in their sight" (*kalē sphodra* = beautiful greatly/exceedingly)
- LOGOS: "strikingly beautiful to their eyes"
- PNEUMA: "stunning"
- SOPHIA ruling: "exceedingly beautiful in their sight" — *sphodra* = exceedingly; neither "strikingly" nor "wonderfully" captures the Greek adverb as precisely

**21. v. 15 — "you have saved your life by hastening down"**
- EMET: "you have saved your-life by-hastening-down to come before our lord"
- LOGOS: "you have saved your life by coming down at once to present yourself to our lord"
- PNEUMA: "You just saved your life by coming down here yourself"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — "coming down at once" preserves the urgency of *kataspasasa* (hastening down); PNEUMA is too colloquial

**22. v. 16 — "he will treat you well"**
- EMET: "he will treat-you well"
- LOGOS: "he will deal with you generously"
- PNEUMA: "he will treat you well"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — "deal with you generously" (*eu poiēsei se*) is more dignified than "treat you well"

**23. v. 18 — "announced from tent to tent"**
- EMET: "her arrival was-announced-from-tent-to-tent"
- LOGOS: "the news of her arrival traveled from tent to tent"
- PNEUMA: "Tent to tent — a woman had come in"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — most naturally conveys *diēggelē apo skēnēs eis skēnēn*

**24. v. 19 — "who can despise this people?"**
- EMET: "who can-despise this people who have women-of-such-kind among them"
- LOGOS: "Who could despise a people that has women like this?"
- PNEUMA: "Who could ever write off a nation with women like that?"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — "despise a people" preserves the national assessment; PNEUMA's "write off a nation" is idiomatic but anachronistic

**25. v. 19 — "those-who-are-released would be able to deceive all the earth"**
- EMET: "those-who-are-released would-be-able to-deceive all the-earth"
- LOGOS: "if we let them go, they would be able to outwit the whole earth"
- PNEUMA: "they will outsmart the whole world"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — "outwit" is a reasonable rendering of *exapatēsai*; "the whole earth" over "the world"

**26. v. 22 — "silver lamps were going before him"**
- EMET: "silver lamps were-going-before him"
- LOGOS: "with silver lamps carried before him"
- PNEUMA: "silver lamps blazing ahead of him"
- SOPHIA ruling: "with silver lamps carried before him" (LOGOS) — PNEUMA's "blazing" introduces detail not in the text

**27. v. 23 — "sheer beauty... was a blow" (PNEUMA) vs. "marveled at the beauty of her face"**
- EMET: "they all marveled at the beauty of her face"
- LOGOS: "they all marveled at the beauty of her face"
- PNEUMA: "the sheer beauty of it was a blow"
- SOPHIA ruling: EMET/LOGOS — PNEUMA's "blow" metaphor is striking and accurate to the narrative function of Judith's beauty but is interpretive; the Greek *ethaumasan* = they marveled/wondered
